subject: colonization and extinction both increase with increasing values of a covariate

messages.author: d4faea1b8de234dc
messages.subject: colonization and extinction both increase with increasing values of a covariate
parts:
We are using colext for multi-season occupancy modeling for point count observations of birds. 

To visualize some of our results for one of the species, we have graphed predicted values of a Vegetation Variable Y (specifically, basal area of two tree species at each point) against gamma and epsilon separately for each year (the parameter estimate for this variable is significant in both gamma and epsilon models). 

What I notice is that the probability of both colonization AND extinction increase across the same range of the vegetation variable (basal area of two tree species) in at least some of the same years. This seems biologically odd to me, if I am understanding correctly, as we would interpret these results as "If a site is unoccupied, the probability of it being colonized increases with increasing  basal area" but also "If this site is occupied, the probability of it becoming unoccupied increases with increasing basal area." It would make more sense biologically to me if one probability was positively associate with the veg variable and the other were negatively related (or not related at all). 

Is there any reason to think that this points to something wrong in our analysis?

Some background: Because there were multiple best models (delta AIC < 2), we used model-averaging to calculate predicted values. To get predicted values of gamma and epsilon for a given variable, we calculated values across the range of observed values for that variable, while other variables were assigned their mean observed value.

Thanks for any thoughts on this....

Sharon

messages.author: 527d9b3ec7deff2d
messages.subject: Re: colonization and extinction both increase with increasing values of a covariate
parts: Well, if sites with high basal area are frequently changing states between years then it is not surprising for colonization and extinction to be correlated.  This just means that sites are not staying open or closed for very long.  I suppose it could also indicate a problem with closure if your high basal area sites were truly always "occupied" in that the species was in the general area but was not available for detection in some years.  This is a common problem for birds, depending on the sampling design.
